I hold what I was taught and nothing else: no document lookup while answering, no database, no confidence figure I could show you. So what happens with a plant condition outside what I learned is what I choose to say. I tell you I do not know it. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just the sick cow. The veterinary service will provide the correct medication.

Remember the plan asks for at least five compartments in all, so you will still need the brooding compartment, the chick room and a second grower space, plus a grassy run and a store outside. Take the division to ICAT before you build the partitions.

history.content: I want to know whether my building is big enough.

Give me two things: the inside measurements, and the ages of the birds you want to put in it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA commercial reference works on 8 to 10 birds per square metre for breeders, 50 for chicks and 12 to 15 for the growers, and the 2017 ESFT village compendium works on 5 to 6 hens per square metre for the improved family henhouse, so I also need to know which of the two you are building.
Seven metres by four, the commercial model, and I want breeders and growers both.

draws.answer: Then you are at the middle of the two. Breeders, 8 to 10 per square metre, are 140 birds at the commercial model and 42 at the family henhouse, and a brooding hen needs 10 to 12 months of incubation, which takes up most of the space. The growers, 50 at 5 to 6, are 21 to 25 per square metre. Count your 7 m by 4 m and put the densities: two groups of 7 m by 4 m by 1.5 m for the breeders, and two groups of 7 m by 4 m by 1.5 m for the growers, so you are right where you want. Work out the net result: 140 times 7 for the breeders, 196 times 7 for the growers, so 2,420 birds for seven by four, a figure you can use to build the budget. And then the count: 2,420 birds divided by 125 is about 19 breeding cycles a year, and three production cycles a year for the growers.

Then you are taking the breeders figure, 8 to 10 per square metre, with a smaller footprint: 7 by 4 is 28 square metres, so 28 times 10 equals 280 birds. And count the ages next, because it is the same reference that sets the densities by age: breeders 50 to 60 and growers 12 to 15. So at 280 square metres you are over by about 70 birds on average, which is why it says to plan for space and not for numbers. Take that figure to ICAT or ITRA and put the ages you actually expect.

per_item.reference: No. More urea than recommended does not give more maize: over-dosing wastes your money and can even cut the yield. For maize, the ITRA and ICAT fiche gives about 100 kg of urea per hectare, put at panicle initiation, 30 to 45 days after sowing, in a pocket away from the stem so it does not burn the plant. What raises the harvest is putting the right amount at the right time, after the base NPK, and keeping the weeding on schedule. If you think your soil needs more, ask ICAT for an adjustment to your soil.

per_item.reference: No, the cycles overlap. A bird takes twenty-one days of incubation and then six months to reach sale weight, about 1.3 kg for a hen and 1.5 kg for a cock, so no bird goes from egg to sale in two months. Six production cycles a year in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference means six settings running at different stages at the same time: one batch in the incubator or under hens, one in the brooder for its first three weeks, one in the chick room, others in the grower compartments for the 3 to 6 month birds. That is also why the reference asks for at least five compartments: several ages are on the farm at once by design.

history.content: Six cycles a year means a bird goes from egg to sale in two months.

draws.answer: Not two months. The six production cycles a year in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference are one cock for ten hens and one brooder for the chicks, with the first three birds taking 28 days, the second three taking 30, the chick brooder used for their first three weeks and then the local henhouse for the adults. That is a cycle, not a line of time, and it is also a size rather than a speed: at that flock size each bird takes about ten eggs in the brooder and leaves them eight to ten days at most in the same reference.

It is closer, but the figures are not the same. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on six production cycles a year, about ten eggs laid per hen per laying, about six layings a year, a natural hatching rate near seventy percent and a mortality rate near ten percent, all in 2020 prices. Six cycles would mean that number approaches seven. What changes is the projection: the annual projection in the same study runs to 1,422 birds at 2,250 FCFA in the first year and 2,376 birds at 2,250 FCFA in the second. Six cycles carries a second year. The selling time is also different: the same study projects a first year selling 1,422 birds at 2,250 FCFA and a second year selling 2,376 birds at 2,250 FCFA, both in 2020 prices. So the two are not the same bird.

per_item.reference: Look under the leaves of your tomato plants every week to detect any tiny insects. Turn each leaf over and count the insects on a few plants before you decide on any spray. If the insects are numerous, prune the most infested leaves and destroy them. Remove weeds from the plot edges that can serve as a refuge for the pests. Use yellow sticky traps for whiteflies and a strong water jet to wash off aphids, while ladybirds and lacewings will naturally suppress them. For the approved product and dosage, contact ICAT.

history.content: The leaves on my tomatoes are yellowing and I hear a faint buzzing, what's the first thing I should do?

draws.answer: Those signs point to whiteflies or aphids attacking your tomato crop. Begin by shaking each tomato plant and inspecting the undersides of several leaves to identify which pest is present, because the measures differ. Turn the leaves over and count the insects on a few plants before deciding to treat. If you find many whiteflies, set yellow sticky traps to catch the adults. If aphids are dominant, spray a strong jet of water on the foliage and encourage natural enemies such as ladybirds and lacewings. Remove and destroy the most infested leaves and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the pests. For a heavy infestation, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

The first thing you should do is turn the tomato leaves over and count the insects on a few plants to confirm the presence of the sucking pests. Then shake each tomato plant and inspect it before you spray, because the wrong name wastes spray and money. Pick the most infested tomato leaves and destroy them, and clear weeds around the plot that can host the insects. If the insect count is high, you may need to contact ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

per_item.reference: From the Ministry and PASA catalogue of good practices. Year one, improving plants, the legumes that feed the soil with nitrogen: beans, groundnut, cowpea. Year two, a hungry plant that consumes a lot, maize, the soil now being rich in nitrogen. Year three, a root or tuber crop that goes for the nutrients left deeper, yam. Year four, an undemanding plant such as a leafy vegetable, okra. Then back to year one with legumes. Before fixing it, take account of your soil's fertility and of last season's crop.

history.content: rotation 4 ans exemple

draws.answer: Year 1: legumes, year 2: maize. Then year 3: a root or tuber crop, year 4: an undemanding plant such as a leafy vegetable. That is what the ITRA and ICAT maize brochure puts the maize in between two legumes each year. The maize is the hungry plant, the legumes the nitrogen fixers that feed the soil with it. The brochure pairs a nitrogen-fixing legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean with a hungry crop like maize, and puts the maize at the head of the rotation so the nitrogen it has gained can feed the next crop. Before fixing a rotation, take account of the fertility of the soil and of what grew there last season.

Year 1, legumes, year 2, maize: the catalogue says maize is a rooting plant, it goes down, the nitrogen it takes is from the soil, so it is a hungry plant that takes what is left. Year 3, a hungry plant, a root or tuber crop, the soil is now rich in nitrogen, so it needs less: yam, cassava, yacouboua. Year 4, an undemanding plant, an undemanding crop, a leafy harvest at the peak, the soil is now rich in nitrogen again, so it returns to the soil with a yield. That is the four year example it gives. The brochure's rule is the same in both cases: maize at the head of the rotation, then a legume, then a root crop, then an undemanding plant.

per_item.reference: Transplant seedlings after about 21 days in the nursery, placing 2 to 3 plants per pocket spaced 20 by 20 centimetres. For lowland or irrigated fields, apply 200 kilograms per hectare of NPK 15-15-15 about a week after transplanting, then split 100 kilograms per hectare of urea, giving half at tillering and half at panicle initiation. Weed the field at 15 to 25 days after transplanting and again around 40 days. Protect the crop from birds from flowering until harvest. If you need variety matching or rate adjustments, see ICAT.

history.content: How should I transplant and fertilise my rice seedlings?

draws.answer: Transplant seedlings after about 21 days in the nursery, placing two to three plants per pocket spaced 20 by 20 cm. Use fertile, well-drained soil, creating a pocket 10-15 cm deep with 5-10 cm of treated fungicide seed powder. After transplant, spread NPK 15-15-15 at 200 kg per hectare about a week after planting, then spread urea at 100 kg per hectare split in two equal applications, the first at tillering and the second at panicle initiation. Weed the field at 15-25 days and again around 40 days after transplanting. Guard the crop against birds from flowering to harvest. For variety matching and exact fertiliser amounts, see ICAT.

Transplant the rice seedlings at 20 by 20 centimetre spacing. First, establish a close spacing of 80 cm for lowland rice and 10 cm for highland rice, then thin the seedlings to 5 by 5 cm when they are 3 to 5 days old. After thinning, apply NPK fertilizer at 200 kg per hectare in a pocket 5 to 10 cm from each plant, keeping the fertilizer away from the plant to prevent burn. Keep the field weed-free to reduce aphid hosts. For variety selection and dose adjustments, consult ICAT.

per_item.reference: It is not a pest problem; the maize is experiencing nitrogen depletion on a soil that has lost organic matter. First, look at the leaves: uniform pale yellow on the older lower leaves indicates nitrogen hunger. Second, avoid buying a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide based on a merchant's word, because mineral fertilizer alone often does not give a return on exhausted soil. Third, restore organic matter by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Fourth, plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the proper dose for your plot. ICAT is the service to see.

history.content: My old maize field in Kara shows pale yellow older leavees while the new ones stay green, is it a pest?

draws.answer: That pattern is a sign of nitrogen shortage in your maize crop. Start by reading the leaves; the uniform pale yellow on the older lower leaves means the plant is hungry for nitrogen, not suffering from a disease. Then, avoid purchasing a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide on a merchant's recommendation because mineral fertilizer alone often fails on run-down soil. Next, bring organic matter back by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues in the soil instead of burning them. After that, plant a legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct dose for your plot. ICAT is the service to see.

per_item.reference: Then the count against the floor may be fine and the compartment still wrong. Check the number first: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on 8 to 10 breeders per square metre, 12 to 15 growers and 50 chicks, so measure and divide before anything else. If you are inside the figure, look at why one end is unused. The reference wants the henhouse well aired and roomy, with a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m, three bricks at most, and tarpaulins kept to close against rain and wind, so a cold or wet end will empty. Check the feeders and drinkers are spread rather than grouped: for adults, one feeder of 150 cm by 12 by 16 for 25 birds, and four drinkers of 10 litres per hundred layers. And keep the compartments to their ages, since that is what the five compartment plan is for.

history.content: The birds are crowded at one end and the other end stays empty.

draws.answer: Then the compartment is not the right size, and the method is exactly what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks. Keep breeders at 8 to 10 breeders per square metre. If you have a breeder compartment, its floor must be raised: tarpaulins are for rain and wind, but a henhouse opening onto a room that has no roof is a shelter rather than a breeder compartment. The compartment should be well aired and roomy, with the drinkers and the feeder at the floor level so the chicks do not have to climb. And wash the inside, because a good cleaning already removes a good part of the germs.

That is the trouble the compartment is meant to solve, and the answer is the one the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives. It says to provide at least five compartments in the henhouse so the birds do not crowd: breeder, chick and grower, and two compartmented for the breeders at one end and the growers at the other, with the breeder compartment walled high with an apatam over it, and tarpaulins kept in for rain and wind. So do not let the birds wander, and keep the ground clear inside, since a tuft of grass shelters the rats, shrews, snakes, ants and other creatures that bring disease. And take the floor to ICAT, which is the office for the plans scaled to your flock.

per_item.reference: The symptom is nitrogen loss in maize, not a disease that requires roguing. Start by opening a shallow drainage channel so water runs off the plot instead of standing. When the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, applying about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation, and keep the fertilizer off the plant to avoid burn. Continue with the second weeding and earthing-up as scheduled. If you later see streaks or dead-hearts, you should see ICAT.

history.content: After a heavy shower my corn's lower leaves are pale, especially where water pooled. Should I remove the plants?

draws.answer: The pale lower leaves of your maize after heavy rain indicate nitrogen loss, not a disease. Open a shallow drainage channel to let excess water run off the plot. Once the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, applying roughly 100 kg per hectare at the panicle initiation stage, and keep the fertilizer away from the plant to avoid burn. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule as planned. If you later observe any streaks or dead-hearts, consult ICAT.

per_item.reference: It is bloat affecting your nanny goat. Immediately get the goat on its feet and keep it moving, holding its head raised to help belching. After that, drench a little vegetable or mineral oil into its mouth to break the froth and free the gas. This helps the rumen work again and lets the gas escape. The condition can lead to collapse very quickly. Call the veterinary service immediately for emergency assistance.

history.content: My nanny goat's left flank is tight, she stopped grazing and looks like she is struggling to breathe.

draws.answer: Is she also showing a swollen throat or has the left flank turned dull?

Your nanny goat is experiencing bloat, an emergency condition. First, get the goat standing and moving, keeping its head raised so it can belch the trapped gas. Next, drench a small amount of vegetable or mineral oil by mouth to break the froth and let the gas escape. Call the veterinary service immediately because a severe case needs their immediate intervention. The veterinary service is the appropriate contact for this emergency.

per_item.reference: Your cattle have gall sickness (anaplasmosis). Call the veterinary service the same day because only they can confirm the disease and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet that the urine is yellow-brown without red, which points to gall sickness. Keep the sick animal in the shade, give it clean water within reach, and do not make it walk because it lacks red blood cells. Hand-pick all ticks you can see on the whole herd, not just the sick animal, to stop further spread. See the veterinary service the same day.

history.content: My cows are looking weak, they have yellow urine and seem to lag behind the herd.
Are the gums and eyelids pale or white?
Yes, their gums and eyelids are pale.

draws.answer: Your cattle likely have gall sickness caused by Anaplasma marginale. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can confirm the disease and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine, yellow-brown without red, which points to gall sickness. Keep the sick animal in the shade, provide clean water, and avoid making it walk because it is short of red blood cells. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just the sick animal, since ticks on other cattle can spread the parasite. See the veterinary service the same day.

Your cattle have redwater caused by Babesia. Call the veterinary service the same day and tell them the urine is red to black, which points to redwater. Keep the sick animal in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not only on the sick animal. The veterinary service will confirm the disease and give the correct drug and dose. You must see the veterinary service the same day.

per_item.reference: Waiting with a small bag of beans after the harvest can be profitable. First, make sure the beans are stored well dried to keep them in good condition. Then keep that bag instead of selling the whole harvest immediately. When the lean season arrives, roughly June through August, prices usually go up. Check the weekly market day for your village and follow SIM cereal price updates on the radio before you decide to sell. Compare the local price plus transport cost with the price you might achieve in Lomé or other large markets. If you can, join a cooperative or sell together to reach larger buyers and cut per-bag transport cost. For more assistance, approach a cooperative or ICAT, and also ANSAT for grain.

history.content: I have a small bag of beans left after harvest. Is it smart to wait before selling?

draws.answer: The guidance is to sell after the harvest glut, not during the harvest rush. First, store your beans well-dried to keep them in the season. Then, gather all your beans and other cereal grain and store them together in a closed, sealed container. This way, the grain does not lose its quality. Next, take some of the dried grain to ICAT for advice on selling as a group or cooperative, which can often bring the price up. Remember that the price you pay on local markets is usually lower than what you could get in Lome or other large urban markets. For the best current outlet, contact a cooperative or ICAT.

Selling your bean bag at harvest is the normal practice, and waiting is not smart; you are selling at the glut. But do not ignore the price you get. Record every expense, work out the cost of production per 100 kg, decide the profit you want per 100 kg, compare that price with the market price, and readjust if needed. Store your beans well dried and, if possible, hold part of the harvest to sell in the lean season when prices rise. For this season's outlet, go to SIM's weekly market days and ask ICAT what price you can reach.
